short: Paying back part or all of a loan before its scheduled end, which cuts the total interest you pay over the loan's life.
kid: You borrowed sweets from a friend and give a few back each week, plus one thank-you sweet every week. If you pay them all back early, you stop owing the thank-you sweets.
detail: Loan prepayment means repaying principal ahead of the agreed schedule, either in part (a part-prepayment) or in full, which Indian lenders call foreclosure or pre-closure. Because interest is charged on the outstanding balance, every rupee prepaid stops attracting interest for the rest of the loan. After a part-prepayment the borrower usually chooses between keeping the EMI and shortening the tenure, which saves the most interest, or keeping the tenure and lowering the EMI. Under RBI rules as of 2025, banks and NBFCs cannot charge prepayment penalties on floating-rate loans taken by individuals for non-business purposes, while fixed-rate loans may still carry a fee. Watch the wording: in India foreclosure means closing your own loan early, but in the US it means a lender seizing a home after missed payments. Prepaying makes most sense when the loan rate is higher than what the money could safely earn elsewhere.
example: Say Arjun owes ₹30 lakh on a home loan at 9% a year with 15 years left, so his EMI is about ₹30,428. If he prepays ₹5 lakh and keeps the same EMI, the loan ends in about 129 months instead of 180 and he saves roughly ₹10.8 lakh of interest. If he keeps the tenure and lowers the EMI to about ₹25,357 instead, he saves only about ₹4.1 lakh.

short: A contract where you pay regular amounts to an insurer, and it pays a fixed sum to your family if you die during the policy.
kid: A parent gives a helper a few coins every year. If the parent is ever gone, the helper gives the family a big bag of money so they still have food and a home.
detail: Life insurance is a contract in which the policyholder pays premiums and the insurer promises a payout, the sum assured, to the nominees if the insured person dies during the policy term. Pure protection plans (term insurance) pay only on death; savings-linked plans such as endowment policies, money-back plans and ULIPs also pay if the insured survives to maturity, which makes them far costlier for the same cover. Insurers pool mortality risk across many lives and invest premiums largely in government bonds, which makes life insurers some of the biggest long-term buyers in India's bond market. LIC remains the largest player, alongside private insurers, many of them bank-promoted. A common rule of thumb is cover of 10 to 15 times annual income for anyone with dependants. The usual confusion: life insurance protects dependants and is not an investment; mixing the two often means too little cover and low returns.
example: Say Neha, 30, earns ₹8 lakh a year and supports her parents. A rule of thumb of 10 to 15 times income suggests cover of ₹80 lakh to ₹1.2 crore. If she buys a ₹1 crore policy and dies during its term, her nominees receive ₹1 crore.
formula: Rough cover needed = Annual income x 10 to 15 (rule of thumb)

short: Pure life insurance for a fixed period: small yearly premiums, and a large payout to your family only if you die within that period.
kid: You give a helper a few coins every year. If you are ever gone, the helper gives your family a big treasure chest. If you are fine, the helper keeps the coins, like an umbrella you carried on a day it never rained.
detail: Term insurance is life cover for a fixed term that pays the sum assured to nominees only if the insured dies within that term. If the policyholder survives, nothing is paid, which is why it is the cheapest way to buy large cover: the premium pays only for mortality risk, with no savings element. Premiums depend on age, health, smoking, cover and term, and are usually locked in at purchase, so buying young costs less. Planners often suggest buying term cover and investing the difference separately rather than buying an endowment plan or ULIP. Honest disclosure matters: within three years of the policy date a claim can be rejected for fraud or hidden facts such as illness or smoking; after that, Section 45 of the Insurance Act bars the insurer from questioning the policy on any ground. Common confusion: getting nothing back is not a loss; you bought protection.
example: Say a healthy 25-year-old non-smoker buys ₹1 crore of cover for 35 years at ₹12,000 a year. Over the full term she pays ₹4.2 lakh in premiums. If she dies at 50, her nominee receives ₹1 crore; if she lives past 60, the policy simply ends.

short: Insurance that pays hospital and medical bills, up to a chosen limit, when you fall ill or get injured, in return for a yearly premium.
kid: Getting really sick can mean a big hospital bill. This is like a friend who promises to help pay the doctor, so your family does not have to empty the piggy bank.
detail: Health insurance pays for medical treatment, mainly hospitalisation, day-care procedures and costs just before and after a hospital stay, up to the sum insured chosen for the policy year. Most Indian retail plans are indemnity policies: they pay actual admissible costs, not a fixed amount, either cashless at network hospitals or by reimbursement. Terms that change how much you really get include room-rent limits, co-payment, waiting periods for pre-existing diseases, sub-limits on specific treatments and the no-claim bonus. IRDAI reforms in 2024 removed the upper age limit for buying a policy and capped the pre-existing disease waiting period at three years. Under the old tax regime, as of 2025, premiums qualify for a deduction under Section 80D of the Income-tax Act, 1961. Common confusion: employer group cover ends when you leave the job, so a personal policy bought young protects continuity. Mediclaim is an older name for basic hospitalisation cover.
example: Say Rohan has a ₹5 lakh policy and is hospitalised with a bill of ₹3.2 lakh, of which ₹8,000 is for items the policy excludes, such as gloves and admission kits. The insurer pays ₹3.12 lakh and Rohan pays ₹8,000. His remaining cover for the year is ₹1.88 lakh.

short: A health insurance policy where one shared cover amount protects the whole family, and any member can use it in a year.
kid: A family keeps one big jar of sweets for whenever anyone feels poorly. Anyone can take from it, but if one person takes a lot, less is left for everyone else.
detail: A family floater is a single health policy covering several family members, typically self, spouse, children and sometimes parents, under one sum insured that any member can use during the policy year. It is cheaper than separate individual policies of the same size because the insurer assumes that not everyone will fall ill in the same year. The premium depends mainly on the age of the eldest member, so adding senior parents can raise the cost sharply; many planners keep parents on a separate policy. Restoration or recharge benefits refill the cover after it is used up, often only for a different illness or a different member. The common confusion: a ₹10 lakh floater for four people is ₹10 lakh shared, not ₹10 lakh each, so one major illness can exhaust protection for the whole family that year.
example: Say a family of four buys a ₹10 lakh floater. In March the father's surgery costs ₹6 lakh, which the policy pays. For the rest of that policy year, all four members share the remaining ₹4 lakh, unless the plan has a restoration benefit.

short: Extra health cover that starts paying only after your total hospital bills in a year cross a set amount, called the deductible.
kid: Your own piggy bank pays for small scrapes and bumps. If the bills get really big, a second, bigger piggy bank opens up and pays the rest.
detail: A super top-up is a health policy that pays only once your total admissible medical bills in a policy year exceed a threshold, the deductible, which is usually set equal to your base cover. Because the insurer never pays the first slice of costs, a large super top-up costs far less than raising the base sum insured by the same amount, making it a popular way to build ₹20 lakh to ₹1 crore of protection. The key difference from a plain top-up: a top-up applies the deductible to each claim separately, while a super top-up adds up all claims in the year, so several mid-sized hospital stays can still trigger it. The deductible can be met by your base policy, an employer's group cover or your own pocket. Check that waiting periods and room-rent rules in both policies line up.
example: Say Priya has a ₹5 lakh base policy and a ₹20 lakh super top-up with a ₹5 lakh deductible. In one year she has two hospital stays costing ₹3 lakh and ₹4 lakh. The base policy pays ₹5 lakh in total and the super top-up pays the remaining ₹2 lakh; a plain top-up with a ₹5 lakh per-claim deductible would have paid nothing, since neither bill crossed ₹5 lakh.
formula: Super top-up payout = Total admissible bills in the year - Deductible (up to the super top-up sum insured)

short: An optional add-on bought with a main insurance policy for a small extra premium, giving extra protection such as accident or illness cover.
kid: You buy an ice cream cone, and for one more coin you can add sprinkles on top. A rider is the sprinkles: a small extra added to the main thing.
detail: A rider is a supplementary benefit attached to a base life or health policy for an additional premium. Common riders in India include accidental death benefit (an extra payout if death is caused by an accident), critical illness (a lump sum on diagnosis of listed diseases), accidental disability, hospital cash, and waiver of premium, under which future premiums are waived if the policyholder becomes disabled or critically ill or, in child plans, if the paying parent dies. Riders usually cost less than buying the same cover as a standalone policy, but they end when the base policy ends or lapses, and their cover is often capped relative to the base sum assured. The common confusion: a rider does not change the base policy's terms; it pays only for the specific event it names, under its own definitions, waiting periods and exclusions, so read them separately.
example: Say Karan has a ₹1 crore term policy at ₹12,000 a year and adds a ₹50 lakh accidental death rider for ₹1,500 more, paying ₹13,500 in total. If he dies in a road accident during the term, his nominee receives ₹1.5 crore; if he dies of an illness, the nominee receives ₹1 crore.

short: A policy that combines life insurance with market investing: part of each premium buys cover and the rest goes into funds you choose.
kid: You give a helper some coins. The helper keeps a few to protect your family and plants the rest in a garden that may grow big or small.
detail: A ULIP is a life insurance product in which premiums, after charges, buy units of equity, debt or balanced funds chosen by the policyholder, much like a mutual fund, while a life cover runs alongside. The fund value moves with the net asset value of the chosen funds, so the investment risk sits with the policyholder. Charges include premium allocation, policy administration, mortality (the cost of the life cover, recovered by cancelling units) and fund management, which IRDAI rules as of 2025 cap at 1.35% a year. ULIPs carry a five-year lock-in; surrender earlier and the money moves to a discontinued policy fund until year five. Under tax rules as of 2025, maturity proceeds are tax-free only if annual premiums stay within ₹2.5 lakh for policies issued from February 2021. Heavy charges in pre-2010 ULIPs fuelled mis-selling, so compare total costs with a term plan plus a mutual fund.
example: Say Ananya pays a ₹1 lakh annual ULIP premium and the premium allocation charge is 2%, or ₹2,000. The remaining ₹98,000 buys units of an equity fund at a NAV of ₹20, giving her 4,900 units. Each month a few units are cancelled to pay mortality and administration charges.
formula: Units allotted = (Premium - Premium allocation charge) / NAV; Fund value = Units held x NAV

short: A life insurance policy that pays a lump sum either when you die during the term or when you survive to the end of it.
kid: You put a coin in a special box every year for many years. At the end you get the coins back with a little extra, and if something happens to you before then, your family gets the box.
detail: An endowment plan is a traditional life insurance policy that pays the sum assured, plus any bonuses, on death during the term or on survival to maturity. Money-back policies are a variant that return slices of the sum assured at fixed intervals, for example every five years, with the balance at maturity. In participating (with-profit) plans, the insurer invests premiums mostly in bonds and declares yearly bonuses that are not guaranteed until added. Because much of the premium funds the savings element, the life cover is small relative to the premium, and long-run returns have often been around 4% to 6% a year, close to or below inflation. Surrendering early usually returns well under the premiums paid. The common confusion: guaranteed does not mean good; compare the plan's internal rate of return with a term plan plus a Public Provident Fund or debt fund over the same period.
example: Say Vikram pays ₹50,000 a year for 20 years, ₹10 lakh in all, into an endowment plan with a ₹10 lakh sum assured, and receives ₹15 lakh at maturity. That works out to a return of only about 3.7% a year. Had he died during the term, his family would have received only ₹10 lakh plus any bonuses added so far.
formula: Maturity benefit = Sum assured + Accrued bonuses (+ Final additional bonus, if any)

short: The price you pay an insurer, as a one-time, monthly or yearly amount, to keep an insurance policy active.
kid: To keep the friendly helper on your side, you give them a few coins every year. Those coins are the small price you pay for the helper's promise.
detail: A premium is the amount a policyholder pays to buy and keep insurance cover. It can be paid as a single lump sum or in regular instalments, and missing it beyond the grace period can make a policy lapse. Insurers price it from expected claims, the pure or risk premium, plus loadings for expenses, commissions, profit and a safety margin. For life cover the key drivers are age, health, smoking, sum assured and term; for health cover, age, city, sum insured and claim history; for motor cover, vehicle value, model and no-claim bonus. Premiums are an insurer's revenue and fund the reserves it invests, which is why analysts track premium growth closely. Under GST rules as of 2025, individual life and health premiums are exempt. Common confusion: a lower premium is not always better value; check the cover, exclusions and claim record behind it.
example: Say an insurer expects 1 in 1,000 healthy 35-year-olds to die in a year. For ₹1 crore of cover, the pure risk premium is ₹10,000 (₹1 crore x 1/1,000). Adding 20% for expenses and profit gives a yearly premium of ₹12,000.
formula: Gross premium = Pure risk premium (Probability of claim x Payout) + Loadings for expenses and profit

short: The amount an insurance policy promises to pay: a fixed sum in life insurance, or a maximum limit on bills in health insurance.
kid: It is the number written on the promise: how many coins the helper will give if something bad happens. It is decided at the very start, before anything goes wrong.
detail: Sum assured is the guaranteed amount a life insurance policy pays on death, or on maturity in savings plans, fixed when the policy is bought. Life cover is a benefit contract: the full amount is paid when the insured event happens, whatever the actual financial loss. Sum insured, the term used in health and general insurance, works differently: it is the maximum the insurer will pay in a policy year, and claims are reimbursed at actual admissible cost, which is called the indemnity principle. Choosing the figure is the key decision: life cover is usually sized to replace years of income and repay debts, and health cover to match hospital costs in your city plus a buffer for medical inflation. The common confusion: a ₹5 lakh health policy does not hand you ₹5 lakh, while a ₹5 lakh life policy does pay ₹5 lakh.
example: Say Meera has a term policy with a ₹50 lakh sum assured and a health policy with a ₹5 lakh sum insured. If she is hospitalised and the bill is ₹2 lakh, the health insurer pays ₹2 lakh, not ₹5 lakh. If she dies during the term, her nominee receives the full ₹50 lakh.

short: The money an insurer pays if you end a savings-type life insurance policy before it matures, usually less than the premiums you paid.
kid: You promised to put a coin in a jar every week for many weeks. If you stop early and ask for the jar back, you get some coins back, but not all of them.
detail: Surrender value is the amount paid when a policyholder voluntarily ends a life insurance policy before maturity. Pure term plans usually have no surrender value; endowment, money-back, whole life plans and ULIPs do. For traditional plans, insurers work out a guaranteed surrender value, a percentage of premiums paid that rises as the policy ages, and a special surrender value based on the paid-up value and bonuses, and pay the higher. The gap between premiums paid and surrender value works as a surrender charge that recovers commissions and costs paid upfront. ULIPs surrendered within five years move to a discontinued policy fund and pay out only after the lock-in. IRDAI's 2024 product rules pushed insurers to offer fairer surrender values in the early years. Common confusion: surrender is not the only exit; making a policy paid-up keeps reduced cover without further premiums, and may be worth more.
example: Say Ravi has paid ₹1 lakh a year for five years into an endowment plan, ₹5 lakh in total, and the insurer quotes a surrender value of ₹3.4 lakh. Surrendering now locks in a loss of ₹1.6 lakh, or 32% of what he paid.
formula: Guaranteed surrender value = Surrender value factor x Total premiums paid (exact rules vary by plan)

short: The share of claims an insurer actually paid out of all claims it decided in a year, used to judge how reliably it pays.
kid: If one hundred friends ask a helper for help and the helper helps ninety-eight of them, that is a very good helper. This number shows how often the helper keeps its promise.
detail: Claim settlement ratio (CSR) is the percentage of claims an insurer settled out of the total it had to decide in a year, usually counted by number of claims and sometimes by amount. IRDAI publishes it for life insurers in its annual report, and buyers use it as a quick check of how reliably an insurer honours death claims; most large Indian life insurers have reported ratios above 95% in recent years. A ratio by number can look high even if a few large claims are rejected, so compare it with the ratio by amount and the share of claims rejected or pending. For health insurers, also look at the incurred claims ratio, which compares claims paid with premiums earned rather than counting approvals. Common confusion: CSR does not measure speed or how much of each bill was paid; partly paid health claims may still count as settled.
example: Say ABC Life had 10,000 death claims to decide in a year, settled 9,850, rejected 100 and left 50 pending. Its claim settlement ratio by number is 98.5% (9,850 / 10,000). If the 100 rejected claims were large policies worth ₹40 crore out of ₹500 crore claimed, its ratio by amount would be at most 92%.
formula: Claim settlement ratio = Claims settled / Total claims to be decided in the year x 100
related: Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India

short: The person you name to receive the money in your bank account, insurance policy or investments if you die.
kid: You write a friend's name on a note and stick it on your toy box. If you ever go away, the grown-ups know to hand the box to that friend.
detail: A nominee is the person or persons named by an account holder or policyholder to receive the proceeds on the holder's death. Nomination is available for bank accounts, fixed deposits, insurance, mutual funds, demat accounts, EPF and NPS, and it lets the institution pay out quickly without demanding a succession certificate. In most cases the nominee is a trustee who holds the money for the legal heirs, who are decided by the will or succession law; Indian courts have repeatedly held that nomination does not override inheritance. Insurance is a partial exception: a spouse, parent or child named as a beneficial nominee gets the money outright. Rules as of 2025 allow up to four nominees on bank accounts and up to ten on demat and mutual fund holdings, with each share specified. Common confusion: a nominee is not the same as an heir, so a will is still needed.
example: Say Meena holds a ₹50 lakh term policy naming her husband and daughter as nominees in a 60:40 ratio. On her death the insurer pays ₹30 lakh to her husband and ₹20 lakh to her daughter, usually within weeks and without a court order.

term: Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India
hl: insurance regulatory and development authority of india
short: India's insurance regulator, set up by law, which licenses insurers and agents, sets rules for policies and protects policyholders.
kid: When lots of helpers promise to look after families, someone has to check that they keep their promises. This is the referee who makes sure the helpers play fair.
detail: IRDAI is the statutory regulator of India's insurance sector, created under the IRDA Act, 1999 and headquartered in Hyderabad. It licenses life, general, health and reinsurance companies and intermediaries such as agents, brokers and banks selling insurance; approves products; sets solvency, investment and disclosure rules; and limits commissions and expenses. It also protects policyholders through claim timelines, free-look periods and grievance redressal via its Bima Bharosa portal, alongside the Insurance Ombudsman. Its stated goal is Insurance for All by 2047, and in 2024 it consolidated dozens of older regulations into a few principle-based ones to widen choice and speed up product approval. For markets, its investment rules shape how insurers deploy premium money in bonds and equities. Common confusion: IRDAI does not settle individual claims or guarantee policies; disputes go first to the insurer, then to Bima Bharosa or the Ombudsman, and finally to consumer courts.
example: Under rules as of 2025, IRDAI requires insurers to keep a solvency ratio of at least 1.5. Say XYZ Insurance has an available solvency margin of ₹3,000 crore against a required margin of ₹1,500 crore, a ratio of 2.0, comfortably above the floor. If losses cut the available margin to ₹2,100 crore, the ratio falls to 1.4 and IRDAI could step in and demand fresh capital.
formula: Solvency ratio = Available solvency margin / Required solvency margin

short: Selling someone a financial product that does not suit their needs, or hiding or misstating its risks, costs or features to make the sale.
kid: A shopkeeper says a toy is magic and will last forever, just so you buy it, but it breaks in a week. Tricking someone into buying the wrong thing is not fair.
detail: Mis-selling is the sale of a financial product through misleading claims, hidden costs or unsuitable advice, such as pitching a long-term insurance plan to an elderly depositor as a fixed deposit, adding insurance or card add-ons to a loan without clear consent, or overstating guaranteed returns. In India it is most often reported in bancassurance, where banks earn commissions for selling insurance and mutual funds to trusting customers. Regulators push back with suitability and disclosure norms, benefit illustrations, commission limits, recorded consent and, for insurance, a 30-day free-look period under IRDAI rules from 2024 in which a new policy can be returned. Mis-selling matters for markets too: it erodes trust and can force expensive refunds, as the UK's payment protection insurance scandal did, costing banks tens of billions of pounds. If mis-sold, complain to the seller first, then the regulator or Ombudsman.
example: Say a 68-year-old depositor is sold a policy needing ₹2 lakh a year for 10 years, ₹20 lakh in all, after being told it is a better FD. If she spots the problem within the 30-day free-look period, she can return it and get back her ₹2 lakh minus small deductions for cover, medical tests and stamp duty. If she surrenders in year two instead, she may get back well under the ₹4 lakh she has paid.
related: Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India

short: The checks a bank, insurer or investment firm must do to confirm who you are and where you live before serving you.
kid: Before a new friend can join the clubhouse, the club checks their name and where they live. That way everyone knows who is really inside.
detail: Know your customer (KYC) is the process by which regulated firms verify a customer's identity and address, understand the nature of their activity and keep records, mainly to prevent money laundering, fraud and terror financing under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002. In India it typically uses PAN plus an officially valid document such as Aadhaar, passport, voter ID or driving licence, and can be done in person, through Aadhaar-based e-KYC or by video. The Central KYC Records Registry, run by CERSAI, stores verified records and issues a 14-digit KYC identifier so customers need not repeat the process. Banks also run periodic re-KYC based on risk: under RBI rules as of 2025, at least every 2 years for high-risk, 8 for medium-risk and 10 for low-risk customers. Common confusion: incomplete KYC can freeze a bank account or mutual fund transactions even though the money is still yours.
example: Say Sana opened a savings account in 2016 as a low-risk customer. Under RBI's 10-year cycle for low-risk customers, her bank must complete re-KYC by 2026; if her details have not changed, a simple self-declaration through net banking, an ATM or email usually suffices.

short: A 10-character ID from India's Income Tax Department that ties a person's or company's income, taxes and large money transactions together.
kid: Every child in class has a roll number, so the teacher never mixes up whose homework is whose. This is a roll number for money, so the country can tell whose coins are whose.
detail: PAN is a unique 10-character alphanumeric identifier issued by the Income Tax Department to individuals, companies, firms and trusts. Its format is five letters, four digits and a final check letter; the fourth letter shows the holder type (P for an individual, C for a company, H for a Hindu undivided family) and the fifth is usually the first letter of the surname or name. PAN is needed to file returns, open bank and demat accounts, buy mutual funds and make high-value transactions such as large cash deposits or property purchases, letting the tax department match income with spending. Without a valid PAN, tax is often deducted at a higher rate. An individual's PAN becomes inoperative if not linked with Aadhaar. The PAN 2.0 project, approved in 2024, is upgrading the system with QR-code cards. Common confusion: a person may hold only one PAN; having two can attract a penalty.
example: Say Rahul earns ₹60,000 of fixed deposit interest in a year but never gave his bank his PAN. Under the rules as of 2025, tax can be deducted at 20%, or ₹12,000, instead of the usual 10%, or ₹6,000. He can claim the excess back when filing his return, but that money is stuck until then.

short: A 12-digit identity number issued to every Indian resident who enrols, backed by fingerprints, iris scans and a photo.
kid: Everyone gets their own special number, matched to their fingerprints, which nobody else in the world has. So when you say who you are, a machine can check it really is you.
detail: Aadhaar is a 12-digit unique identity number issued by the Unique Identification Authority of India (UIDAI) under the Aadhaar Act, 2016, linked to a resident's biometrics (ten fingerprints, both irises and a photo) and basic details. By 2025 more than 130 crore numbers had been generated, making it the world's largest biometric ID system. It powers e-KYC for bank accounts, SIM cards and mutual funds, direct benefit transfers of subsidies and Aadhaar-enabled payments, and it is the A in the JAM trinity with Jan Dhan accounts and mobile phones. In 2018 the Supreme Court upheld it for welfare schemes and PAN linkage but struck down mandatory linking with bank accounts and mobile numbers. PAN-Aadhaar linking is compulsory for most individuals; an unlinked PAN becomes inoperative. Common confusion: Aadhaar proves identity and residence, not citizenship, and residents rather than only citizens can hold one.
example: A masked Aadhaar shows only the last 4 of its 12 digits and hides the other 8, so it is the safer copy to share for KYC. Under the rules as of 2025, a person who missed the 30 June 2023 deadline to link PAN with Aadhaar must pay a ₹1,000 fee to link them and make the PAN operative again.

short: A loan whose interest rate goes up or down with a reference rate, such as the central bank's policy rate, unlike a fixed-rate loan.
kid: You borrow a bike and give back sweets each week to say thank you. In one deal the number of sweets can go up or down as sweet prices change; in the other it stays the same every week.
detail: A floating rate loan carries an interest rate that resets periodically in line with a benchmark, while a fixed rate loan keeps the same rate for the full term or an initial period. In India, banks must link new floating-rate retail and small business loans to an external benchmark, usually the RBI repo rate, under the system introduced in October 2019, with resets at least every three months; older loans may track MCLR. Your rate is the benchmark plus a spread fixed at sanction, so RBI rate cuts reach floating borrowers quickly, and so do hikes. Fixed rates usually start higher, the price of certainty. RBI's 2023 rules require lenders to let borrowers choose a higher EMI or a longer tenure when rates rise and to offer a switch to a fixed rate. Common confusion: many fixed home loans in India are fixed only for the first few years.
example: Say a home loan is priced at a benchmark of 6% plus a spread of 2.5%, so the borrower pays 8.5%. If the RBI cuts the repo rate by 0.25 percentage point and the benchmark follows, the rate falls to 8.25% at the next reset. A fixed rate loan taken the same day at, say, 9.25% would stay at 9.25%.
formula: Floating loan rate = Benchmark rate + Spread

short: A way to charge loan interest only on the amount still owed, so interest falls as you repay, unlike flat-rate interest on the full loan.
kid: You borrowed ten marbles and give one back each week. It is fair to say thank you only for the marbles you still have, not for all ten every single week.
detail: Under the reducing balance method, interest for each period is calculated on the principal still outstanding, so as EMIs repay principal, the interest part of each EMI falls and the principal part rises. Home loans and most bank loans work this way. Under the flat rate method, interest is charged on the original principal for the whole tenure, even after much of it is repaid, so the true cost is far higher than the quoted number: on loans of one to five years, a flat rate matches a reducing balance rate roughly 1.6 to 1.8 times as high. Flat rates still appear in some vehicle, consumer and informal loans. To compare offers, convert everything to a reducing balance rate or the annual percentage rate shown in the lender's Key Fact Statement, which RBI requires. Common confusion: in accounting, the same name describes a depreciation method for assets, not loan interest.
example: Take a ₹1 lakh loan for one year. At a 10% flat rate, interest is ₹10,000 and each of the 12 EMIs is about ₹9,167. At 10% on a reducing balance, the EMI is about ₹8,792 and total interest is about ₹5,499. The flat-rate EMI actually corresponds to a reducing balance rate of about 18% a year.
formula: Flat-rate interest = Principal x Flat rate x Years; Reducing-balance interest for a month = Outstanding principal x (Annual rate / 12)

short: An instalment offer where you pay only the product's price in monthly parts, because the seller covers the lender's interest through a discount.
kid: A shop lets you pay for a toy a little bit each week instead of all at once. The shop quietly pays the extra cost of waiting, so you pay just about the toy's price.
detail: A no-cost EMI lets a buyer pay for a product in equal monthly instalments that add up to the listed price. The loan itself is not interest-free: the lender, usually a card issuer or NBFC, still charges interest, but the brand or retailer funds it by giving an upfront discount equal to the interest, or by paying the lender a fee. RBI warned in 2013 that zero per cent interest schemes can mislead buyers, which is why the structure shows interest offset by a matching discount. Costs remain: 18% GST (as of 2025) on the interest, a possible processing fee, and the loss of any cash discount you might have got by paying upfront. A missed EMI attracts penalties and hurts your credit score, and the EMIs block part of your card limit until repaid. Common confusion: no-cost means no extra cost over the listed price, not no loan.
example: Say a phone costs ₹30,000 on a 6-month no-cost EMI and the card issuer charges 15% a year. The seller gives an upfront discount of about ₹1,270, so the loan is about ₹28,730, repaid in six EMIs of ₹5,000, or ₹30,000 in total. The buyer still pays 18% GST on the ₹1,270 of interest, about ₹229, plus any processing fee.
formula: Upfront discount = Listed price - Present value of the EMIs at the lender's interest rate

short: The most a lender lets you owe at one time on a credit card or credit line.
kid: A friend says you can borrow up to ten marbles at a time, but no more. When you give some back, you can borrow those again.
detail: A credit limit is the maximum outstanding balance a lender allows on a revolving facility such as a credit card or overdraft. The issuer sets it from your income, credit score, existing debts and repayment history, and may raise or cut it later. Available credit is the limit minus what you currently owe, and repayments free up room again. Cash withdrawals usually have a smaller sub-limit and attract interest from day one. Using a large share of your limit, a high credit utilisation ratio, can lower your credit score; many guides suggest staying under about 30%. Under RBI's credit card rules as of 2025, issuers cannot raise your limit or let you go over it without your explicit consent. Common confusion: a higher limit is not extra money; it is borrowing capacity, and interest on unpaid card balances is among the costliest in consumer lending.
example: Say Aditi's card has a ₹1 lakh credit limit and she has spent ₹35,000 this month. Her available credit is ₹65,000 and her utilisation is 35%. Paying ₹15,000 now cuts utilisation to 20% and raises available credit to ₹80,000.
formula: Available credit = Credit limit - Outstanding balance; Utilisation ratio = Outstanding balance / Credit limit x 100

short: A reward from an insurer for not making any claim in a policy year, given as a premium discount or extra cover at renewal.
kid: If you go a whole year without spilling your milk, you get a gold star. Each careful year adds another star.
detail: A no-claim bonus (NCB) rewards a policyholder for each claim-free policy year. In motor insurance it is a discount on the own-damage part of the premium which, on the long-standing Indian scale, rises from 20% after one claim-free year to 50% after five; it belongs to the owner, not the car, so it can move to a new vehicle, but a claim usually resets it to zero. In health insurance it usually takes the form of a cumulative bonus that raises the sum insured, often by 10% to 50% a year up to a cap, at no extra premium. NCB can make small claims a bad trade: claiming ₹5,000 may cost more in lost discount. Common confusion: motor NCB never reduces the third-party premium, and it lapses if renewal is delayed beyond the allowed window, often 90 days after expiry.
example: Say a car's own-damage premium is ₹10,000 and the owner has three claim-free years, earning a 35% NCB. She pays ₹6,500 for own damage instead of ₹10,000. On a ₹5 lakh health policy with a 10% cumulative bonus a year, three claim-free years lift cover to ₹6.5 lakh.
formula: Discounted own-damage premium = Own-damage premium x (1 - NCB %)

short: The fixed share of each health insurance claim that you pay yourself, such as 20%, with the insurer paying the rest.
kid: When you and a friend buy a big pizza, you each pay part of it. Here the helper pays most of the doctor's bill and you pay a small part.
detail: Co-payment is a cost-sharing clause in which the policyholder bears a fixed percentage of every admissible claim and the insurer pays the rest. In India it is common in senior citizen plans, cheaper policies and zone-based plans, where treatment in a costlier city triggers an extra co-pay. A deductible is a different tool: a fixed amount you pay first, per claim or per year, before the insurer pays anything, and it is the basis of top-up and super top-up plans. Both lower premiums because the policyholder carries part of the risk, which also discourages unnecessary claims, a check on moral hazard. Room-rent limits can act as a hidden co-pay because related charges are cut in proportion. Common confusion: in the US a copay usually means a flat fee per doctor visit and the percentage share is called coinsurance; Indian policies use co-pay for the percentage.
example: Say Mr Iyer's policy has a 20% co-payment and his admissible hospital bill is ₹2 lakh. He pays ₹40,000 and the insurer pays ₹1.6 lakh. With a ₹50,000 deductible instead, the insurer would pay ₹1.5 lakh.
formula: Insurer pays = Admissible claim x (1 - Co-payment %); with a deductible, Insurer pays = Admissible claim - Deductible

short: The stretch of time after buying an insurance policy during which certain claims, such as for illnesses you already had, are not paid.
kid: When you join a new game, you sometimes watch for a few turns before you can play. A waiting period is those turns you sit out first.
detail: A waiting period is a span after a policy starts during which specified claims are not covered, to stop people buying insurance only when they already expect to claim. Indian health policies usually have an initial 30-day waiting period for illness (accidents are covered from day one), one to two years for listed conditions such as cataract or hernia, and a waiting period for pre-existing diseases (PED), which IRDAI capped at three years from 2024, down from four. Maternity cover often waits nine months to several years. Waiting periods count from the first policy and carry over when you renew on time or port to another insurer, a key reason to buy early and never let cover break. Common confusion: the waiting period differs from the moratorium, the five-year mark after which a health claim cannot be contested for non-disclosure except for proven fraud.
example: Say Sunil buys a health policy on 1 April 2025 while already diabetic, with a 3-year PED waiting period. A diabetes-related hospitalisation in 2026 will not be covered, but from 1 April 2028 such claims are payable, provided he renews every year without a break. An accident on day one is covered.

short: A health insurance claim where the insurer pays an approved hospital directly, so you pay only items the policy does not cover.
kid: Instead of you paying the doctor and waiting to get your coins back, the helper pays the doctor straight away. You just go home and get better.
detail: In a cashless claim, the insurer or its third-party administrator (TPA) settles the hospital bill directly. The hospital, usually one in the insurer's network, sends a pre-authorisation request with the diagnosis and estimated cost; the insurer approves an amount and gives final approval at discharge, and the patient pays only non-covered items, co-payments or amounts above the limit. In a reimbursement claim, the patient pays first and later submits bills, the discharge summary and reports for repayment, which suits non-network hospitals but ties up cash. IRDAI's 2024 health master circular requires insurers to decide cashless requests within an hour and final discharge approval within three hours. The industry's Cashless Everywhere move lets policyholders seek cashless treatment at non-network hospitals for planned admissions with advance notice. Common confusion: cashless does not mean free; deductions for consumables, room-rent limits and co-pay still apply.
example: Say Farah's bill at a network hospital is ₹2.5 lakh, including ₹12,000 of consumables her policy excludes. Under a cashless claim, the insurer pays the hospital ₹2.38 lakh and she pays ₹12,000 at discharge. Under a reimbursement claim, she would pay all ₹2.5 lakh first and wait to get ₹2.38 lakh back.
related: Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India

short: Insurance that pays a fixed lump sum when you are first diagnosed with a listed serious illness, such as cancer or a heart attack.
kid: If someone gets very, very sick, they may need to rest for a long time and cannot go to work. This helper hands over one big bag of money right away so the family can manage.
detail: Critical illness cover is a benefit policy, sold standalone or as a rider, that pays a pre-agreed lump sum on first diagnosis of a listed illness that meets the policy's definition of severity. Typical lists include specified cancers, heart attack, stroke, kidney failure, major organ transplant, multiple sclerosis and paralysis, and IRDAI has standardised definitions for the most common ones. The payout does not depend on hospital bills, so it can replace lost income, fund treatment or repay loans during a long recovery. Most policies have an initial waiting period of about 90 days and a survival period, often 15 to 30 days after diagnosis, before paying. Because cover usually ends after one payout, it complements rather than replaces health insurance, which reimburses actual bills. Common confusion: early-stage or milder forms of a listed disease may not qualify, so read the definitions closely.
example: Say Deepak has ₹25 lakh of critical illness cover and is diagnosed with a listed cancer. After the 30-day survival period, the insurer pays ₹25 lakh in one go. If his ₹8 lakh treatment bill is reimbursed by his health policy, the full ₹25 lakh is still available to replace income or repay his home loan.

short: All insurance other than life insurance, covering things like vehicles, homes, health, travel, crops and businesses against loss or damage.
kid: If your bike gets scratched or your house gets flooded, this kind of helper pays to fix it. It looks after things, not just people.
detail: General insurance, called non-life or property and casualty insurance abroad, covers losses to property, liability to others and health, usually under one-year contracts that follow the indemnity principle: you are paid for the actual loss, not a fixed sum. Lines include motor, health, fire, marine, engineering, crop, travel, home and liability cover. Motor third-party insurance is compulsory in India under the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, and its premium rates are notified by the government rather than set by each insurer; own-damage cover is optional. The Indian market includes public sector insurers such as New India Assurance, private players and standalone health insurers, with GIC Re as the main domestic reinsurer, and health is now its largest segment by premium. Common confusion: underinsurance is penalised through the average clause, so a home insured for less than its value gets only a proportionate payout.
example: Say a house worth ₹40 lakh is insured for only ₹30 lakh and a fire causes ₹6 lakh of damage. Under the average clause the insurer pays 30/40 of the loss, or ₹4.5 lakh, leaving the owner to bear ₹1.5 lakh. Had the house been insured for its full value, the claim would have paid ₹6 lakh.
formula: Claim under average clause = Loss x (Sum insured / Value of property)
related: Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India

short: Arranging in advance who gets your money and property after you die, and who acts for you if you cannot, mainly through a will.
kid: You write a note saying which friend gets your teddy and who gets your blocks one day. Then nobody has to argue, because your wishes are clear.
detail: Estate planning is deciding how your assets will pass on death and how your affairs will be handled if you become unable to manage them. Core tools are a will naming beneficiaries and an executor, nominations on every account, joint holdings, private trusts for minors or dependants, and powers of attorney. In India a will needs two witnesses but no stamp duty or registration, though registering it helps against disputes; without one, assets pass under personal succession law, such as the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 or the Indian Succession Act, 1925, and heirs may need succession certificates or probate. Muslims can bequeath only up to one-third of their estate by will unless the heirs consent. India has had no estate duty since 1985, unlike the US or UK, which tax large estates. Common confusion: a nominee only collects the money; the will or succession law decides who finally owns it.
example: Say Mr Rao, a Hindu, dies without a will, leaving self-acquired assets of ₹1.2 crore and survived by his wife, mother, son and daughter. Under the Hindu Succession Act these four Class I heirs inherit equally, ₹30 lakh each, whoever the nominee on his accounts was. A will could have divided the estate as he wished.

short: A 12-digit number that stays with an Indian worker for life, linking their provident fund, or retirement savings, accounts from every job.
kid: Each job gives you a new little savings jar. This one special number ties all your jars together with a ribbon, so none get lost when you change jobs.
detail: The Universal Account Number (UAN) is a 12-digit identifier allotted by the Employees' Provident Fund Organisation (EPFO) to every member of the Employees' Provident Fund. Each employer opens a separate member ID for you, but all of them sit under one UAN, which stays with you for life. Introduced in 2014, it lets members view passbooks online, transfer balances when switching jobs, file claims for withdrawals and advances, and keep a continuous service record for the Employees' Pension Scheme. It must be activated and linked with Aadhaar, a bank account and PAN, and a new employer only needs your existing UAN when you join. Common confusion: you should never have two UANs; if an employer creates a new one, the old balance can be stranded until the accounts are merged, and pension service history may break.
example: Say Kavya's basic pay is ₹40,000 a month. Under the rules as of 2025, she contributes 12%, or ₹4,800, and her employer adds ₹4,800, of which ₹1,250 goes to the pension scheme (8.33% of the ₹15,000 wage ceiling) and ₹3,550 to her EPF account. All of it is credited under her single UAN, even after three job changes.

short: A pension savings account under India's National Pension System that parents open and fund for a child, turning into a regular account at 18.
kid: Mum and Dad drop a few coins into a jar for you every year, and the coins slowly grow. When you grow up, the jar becomes yours to keep filling for when you are old.
detail: NPS Vatsalya is a contributory pension scheme for minors, launched in September 2024 and regulated by the Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority (PFRDA). A parent or guardian opens the account in the child's name, with the child as sole beneficiary, and contributes at least ₹1,000 a year with no upper limit; the money is invested by NPS fund managers in equity, corporate bonds and government bonds. When the child turns 18, the account converts to a regular NPS Tier I account. Under PFRDA rules as of 2025, partial withdrawals of up to 25% of contributions are allowed after a three-year lock-in for education, specified illness or disability, and an early exit requires most of a large corpus to buy an annuity. Its strength is decades of compounding. Common confusion: it is a retirement product, not a child education plan, so the money is largely locked up.
example: Say parents put ₹10,000 into NPS Vatsalya at the start of every year from their daughter's birth until she turns 18, ₹1.8 lakh in all. If the money earns 10% a year, which is not guaranteed, the account would hold about ₹5 lakh when it converts to her own NPS account.

short: A pension that promises a set income in retirement based on salary and years worked, unlike a defined contribution plan whose payout depends on investments.
kid: In one deal, your boss promises you a set number of sweets every week when you are old. In the other, you both drop sweets in a jar now, and what you get later depends on how much the jar grows.
detail: A defined benefit (DB) plan promises a retirement income set by a formula, typically an accrual rate times years of service times final or average salary, so the employer or government carries the investment, interest-rate and longevity risk. A defined contribution (DC) plan fixes only what goes in and the payout depends on the fund built up and its returns, so the member bears the risk. India's Old Pension Scheme for government staff is DB; central government employees joining from 1 January 2004 moved to the DC-style National Pension System, and the optional Unified Pension Scheme from April 2025 restores an assured payout. EPF is DC, while the Employees' Pension Scheme is closer to DB. Globally, companies have shifted from DB to DC because DB promises create large, volatile liabilities. Common confusion: a DB pension is only as safe as its sponsor's ability to pay.
example: Say a DB plan pays 2% of final salary for each year of service. After 30 years with a final salary of ₹1 lakh a month, the pension is ₹60,000 a month for life. In a DC plan, saving ₹10,000 a month for 30 years at an assumed 8% a year, compounded monthly, builds about ₹1.49 crore, but the income it buys depends on returns and annuity rates at retirement.
formula: DB pension = Accrual rate x Years of service x Final (or average) salary

short: A group savings-and-borrowing scheme where members pay a fixed amount monthly and one member takes the pooled sum each month.
kid: Ten friends each put one coin in a hat every week. Each week one friend takes the whole hat of coins, until everyone has had a turn.
detail: A chit fund is a rotating savings and credit scheme in which a fixed group of members pays a set instalment every month for a set number of months. Each month the pot goes to one member, usually through an auction in which the member willing to accept the biggest discount wins; the discount, after the organiser's commission, is shared among all members as a dividend that lowers their instalment. Early winners effectively borrow, while late winners effectively save and collect dividends. In India, chit funds are legal when registered under the Chit Funds Act, 1982, which state governments enforce, with the organiser's (foreman's) commission capped at 7% of the chit value since a 2019 amendment; Kerala's state-owned KSFE is a large operator. Common confusion: many collapses called chit fund scams, such as Saradha in 2013, were really unregistered deposit or Ponzi schemes, while informal kitties carry no legal protection.
example: Say 20 members each pay ₹5,000 a month for 20 months, so the monthly pot is ₹1 lakh. In month one, a member who needs cash bids a ₹20,000 discount and receives ₹80,000. The foreman keeps a 5% commission of ₹5,000 and the remaining ₹15,000 is shared as a ₹750 dividend per member, so each pays only ₹4,250 that month.
formula: Dividend per member = (Auction discount - Foreman's commission) / Number of members

short: When those most likely to claim or not repay are the keenest to buy insurance or borrow, because they know more than the seller.
kid: If a shop sells a promise to fix broken toys, the kids who already have wobbly toys rush to buy it first. Then the shop has to fix lots of toys and may run out of coins.
detail: Adverse selection arises when one side of a deal has hidden information before the deal is signed, so the riskiest customers are the most likely to take it up. In insurance, people who expect to fall ill or who smoke are keener to buy cover; if the insurer charges everyone an average price, healthier buyers drop out, average claims rise, premiums rise again, and in the extreme the market shrinks in a death spiral. George Akerlof's 1970 market for lemons paper showed the same logic in used cars, and it applies to lending too, where borrowers willing to pay very high rates may be the riskiest. Insurers fight it with underwriting and medical tests, risk-based pricing, waiting periods, exclusions for pre-existing diseases and group or mandatory cover. Common confusion: adverse selection is about hidden information before the contract, while moral hazard is about behaviour changing after it.
example: Say an insurer has equal numbers of healthy customers expecting ₹5,000 of claims a year and unhealthy ones expecting ₹15,000, and prices everyone at the ₹10,000 average. If only the unhealthy half buys, the average claim jumps to ₹15,000, so the insurer loses ₹5,000 per policy before costs and must raise prices or screen buyers.

short: A measure of how widespread insurance is: total yearly premiums as a share of everything a country produces in a year (GDP).
kid: If you count how many children in a class carry umbrellas, you can tell how ready the class is for rain. This number shows how ready a whole country is for bad days.
detail: Insurance penetration is total insurance premiums written in a year divided by GDP, showing how much of the economy's output goes into buying protection. Insurance density is premiums per person, usually in US dollars, which also reflects income levels. The protection gap is the difference between the cover people need and what they actually hold, for example the family income lost on a breadwinner's death versus life cover in force. IRDAI's annual report put India's penetration at about 3.7% of GDP in 2023-24, mostly life insurance, against a global average near 7%; these figures change every year, so check the latest report. Low penetration signals under-protected households, who fall back on savings or loans in a crisis, and a long growth runway for insurers, central to IRDAI's Insurance for All by 2047 goal. Common confusion: sales of savings-type policies can lift penetration without closing the protection gap.
example: Say a country with a GDP of ₹200 lakh crore and a population of 100 crore collects ₹8 lakh crore of insurance premiums in a year. Its insurance penetration is 4% (₹8 lakh crore / ₹200 lakh crore) and its insurance density is ₹8,000 per person (₹8 lakh crore / 100 crore people).
formula: Insurance penetration = Total premiums / GDP x 100; Insurance density = Total premiums / Population
related: Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India
